newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb court rules against president.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb court rules against president.

text.p: The Bosnian Serb Constitutional Court ruled on Friday against a decision by President Biljana Plavsic to disband the Serb parliament and call early elections.

In a ruling bound to draw widespread international condemnation, it said: "The court has assessed that the said decision is not in harmony with the constitution either in the formal (procedural) sense or in the material (substantial) sense."
The court statement offered few other details of the ruling. Sources said only five of the seven judges voted, four in favour of the ruling and one against.

The court had been expected to strike down Plavsic's move after coming under pressure from government nationalist hardliners loyal to ex-Bosnian Serb president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
The ruling exacerbated a power struggle which erupted between Plavsic and her hardline opponents after she dissolved parliament last month and called general elections in Bosnia's Serb territory.
Plavsic's aides and Western governments had already made clear they were prepared to ignore the court.
Plavsic declined to discuss the court's decision after it was announced on Serb media. "I have not received the official report, so therefore I'm unable to comment," she told Bosnian Serb television.
The office of the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, said earlier this week the court had no legal basis to rescind her decision to disband parliament.

A team of European Union legal experts said the court only had grounds to review whether Plavsic had properly consulted the speaker of the Bosnian Serb parliament and the prime minister before taking the decision.
The United States and European governments have thrown their support behind her because they see her as more willing to cooperate with efforts to enforce a peace treaty.

Although a nationalist ideologue herself, Plavsic has broken with Karadzic and his allies, accusing them running smuggling rackets at the expense of ordinary people and damaging Serb interests by obstructing peace mediators.
Sacked from the ruling party, she formed her own political Serb National Alliance party and pressed ahead with plans to hold early elections, tentatively planned for October.
Plavsic has attracted big crowds at rallies and Western countries hope she and opposition parties can weaken Karadzic's allies in an election.
Shortly before the ruling was announced, the U.S. State Department accused Karadzic's hardliners of trying to manipulate the court.
State Department spokesman James Rubin said the judges were "under intense political pressure to decide this case. And we are aware of specific acts of intimidation."

He added: "The bottom line is that there is a struggle going on in the Republika Srpska between those who are smart enough to realize that compliance with Dayton (peace accords) is the ticket to prosperity and peace for their people, and those leaders who are too stupid to realize that a failure to comply with Dayton, a failure to follow through on the international community's demands will only make their people suffer."

Karadzic's continued freedom is viewed as a major obstacle to a lasting peace in Bosnia. He was indicted during the 1992-95 Bosnian war but no serious effort has been made to arrest him, despite repeated vows by Western powers to bring him before the war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
U.S. President Bill Clinton discussed Bosnia with top foreign policy advisers on Friday and the White House said it was "very important" that Karadzic stand trial for war crimes.
Asked about a Pentagon announcement that there will be a temporary increase in U.S. troops deployed in Bosnia and the message it was sending Karadzic, White House spokesman Mike McCurry replied:
"He should be concerned that the international community is growing increasingly impatient with the inability of the war crimes tribunal to try the case that he has been indicted for."
